421.title: Behar: proclaim liberty (Leviticus 25:8–10)
421.hook: in the fiftieth year, "proclaim liberty throughout the land"
421.howItsDone: The jubilee is not observed today; rabbinic law holds it lapsed when the tribes were exiled. Jews read Behar in synagogue each year, and the jubilee's ideal of release is often cited in Jewish teaching on debt and freedom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shmita: every seventh year the land rests. Your line was the land rests too. Today, what happens after seven of those sevens.

In Philadelphia there's a cracked bell that people line up to see. Around its crown runs an inscription, with a chapter and verse beside it: proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof. It was cast in the 1750s for the Pennsylvania State House. Later, abolitionists adopted it and gave it the name it carries now, the Liberty Bell. The words were already ancient. They come from Leviticus 25, and from a year the Torah calls the yovel.
screen: `A CRACKED BELL IN PHILADELPHIA.` → `THE WORDS AROUND ITS CROWN.` → `LEVITICUS 25.`

segments.voice: Count seven sabbatical years, seven times seven, forty-nine years. Then, on Yom Kippur of the next year, the shofar sounds through the whole land. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout the land unto all the inhabitants thereof; it shall be a jubilee unto you". Land that was sold goes back to the family that held it. Israelites who sold themselves into service go free, home to their families. Every fifty years, the board resets. Now the words. Yovel is the ram's horn; the Talmud says that in Arabia they called a ram yovla. The year is named for the sound that announces it, and through Latin, yovel became our English jubilee. The word for liberty, deror, Rashi explains as the freedom to live wherever you wish, not under someone else's control. Some link it to a bird, the deror, that nests freely wherever it likes. And honesty about history: the Talmud says the jubilee was kept only while all the tribes lived on their land, and stopped once they were exiled. Whether it was ever fully practiced is debated, and the sources are thin. But the idea outlived the practice: land and people aren't meant to be owned forever, and debts and losses shouldn't pass down without end. A bell in Philadelphia carries the words still.

segments.voice: Think of something someone owes you: money, maybe, or an apology you've waited years for, a favor never returned. Ask whether it's time for a jubilee, not because they've earned it, but because fifty years is long enough, or five. Picture deciding, inside, you owe me nothing for this anymore, and notice what changes when the debt is gone.
Yovel. The jubilee: the fiftieth year, announced by the ram's horn, when land returns, people go free, and liberty is proclaimed throughout the land.
Your line: proclaim liberty. The ram's horn sounds for everyone in the land. See you tomorrow.

422.title: Behar: strangers and settlers (Leviticus 25:23)
422.hook: the land is God's, "for ye are strangers and settlers with Me"
422.howItsDone: Behar is read in synagogue in the spring, often paired with Bechukotai. In the Land of Israel some farmers still let fields rest in the seventh year, and the idea that the earth belongs to God shapes Jewish teaching about property and charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday the shofar sounded for the fiftieth year, the yovel. Your line was proclaim liberty. Today, the reason the Torah gives for it.

Somewhere there's a deed with your family's name on it, or a lease, or at least a parking spot you think of as yours. A fence, a title, a signature at a closing table with too many pens. The Torah has paperwork too: fields are bought and sold in Leviticus, with prices worked out by the year. Then, in the middle of all those transactions, God says something that turns every deed into a rental agreement. The field you just paid for was never really for sale.
screen: `A DEED, A LEASE, A FENCE.` → `FIELDS BOUGHT AND SOLD.` → `NEVER REALLY FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: This week's portion is called Behar, on the mountain, because it opens at Sinai. You've met the rest year and the jubilee, when land goes home to the family that first held it. Here is the reason the Torah gives, in Leviticus twenty-five, verse twenty-three: "And the land shall not be sold in perpetuity; for the land is Mine; for ye are strangers and settlers with Me." In Hebrew, gerim v'toshavim. The ger came up three days ago, at one law for all: someone living in a place that isn't originally theirs. A toshav is a settler, someone staying on. Together they make a careful picture: you really live here, you plant and harvest and raise children here, and still, you're a guest. Notice the last word: with Me. Not strangers to God; strangers alongside God, sharing the house with its owner. The same pairing turns up elsewhere. Abraham, buying a burial cave for Sarah, introduces himself to the Hittites as a stranger and a sojourner. A psalm asks God to hear, because the singer is a stranger with God, a sojourner, as all their ancestors were. So the law does two things at once. It protects the poor family that had to sell, because the land comes back. And it reminds the wealthy buyer that they hold a lease, not a crown. Some readers hear a check on pride in it: if even the land is borrowed, so is much of what a person holds.

segments.voice: Pick up something near you that you'd call yours, a phone, a ring, a key, and open your hand flat so it rests on your palm instead of in your grip. Think about where it came from, who made it, how long it will outlast you or how soon it won't. You don't have to give it away; just hold it the way a guest holds a borrowed cup.

423.title: Behar: wronging with words (Leviticus 25:17)
423.hook: the rabbis read "ye shall not wrong one another" as a ban on hurtful words (Bava Metzia 58b)
423.tomorrow: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)
423.howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching treats hurtful speech as a serious wrong; the laws of ona'at devarim, from Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 and the Talmud's discussion at 58b, are studied alongside the laws of gossip, and public embarrassment is treated as a grave harm.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Behar: strangers and settlers with God. Your line was we are guests here. Today, a wrong that doesn't cost a single coin.

A man walks into a pottery shop with no plan to buy anything. He picks up a bowl, turns it over, and asks the owner, how much for this one? Her face lights up. She names a price, starts wrapping it, mentions she made the glaze herself. He shrugs, puts it down, and leaves. Nothing was stolen. Not a coin changed hands. And yet the Mishnah, the early rabbinic law code, lists exactly this moment as a wrong.
screen: `HOW MUCH FOR THIS ONE?` → `NOTHING WAS STOLEN.` → `STILL, A WRONG.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-five says it twice. Verse fourteen, about buying and selling: don't wrong one another. Then verse seventeen: "And ye shall not wrong one another; but thou shalt fear thy God; for I am the LORD your God." The rabbis noticed the repeat. Money was already covered, so, the Talmud says in Bava Metzia fifty-eight b, the second verse must be about words. They called it ona'at devarim, wronging with words. Ona'ah is cheating someone on a price; devarim means words. The Mishnah's examples are startlingly specific. Don't ask the price of something you have no intention of buying: you're raising hope you'll dash. If someone has turned their life around, don't say, remember what you used to do. A teaching quoted in the Talmud adds: if someone is suffering, don't lecture them that they must have earned it, the way Job's friends did. Then the Talmud goes further. Embarrassing someone in public is like shedding blood: you can watch the color drain from their face. It argues that wronging with words is worse than wronging with money, and one reason is simple. Money can be paid back. A word, once it lands, can't be collected. And the verse closes with fear thy God, the same ending that came with the stumbling block. Here it lands on speech. A remark can be passed off as a joke, and only the speaker knows whether it was meant as a knife.
screen: `SAID TWICE: MONEY, THEN WORDS.` · `ONA'AT DEVARIM: CHEATING WITH WORDS.` · `PUBLIC SHAME IS LIKE BLOODSHED.` · `MONEY RETURNS. WORDS DON'T.` · then, large: `YE SHALL NOT WRONG ONE ANOTHER.`

Ona'at devarim. Wronging with words: cheating someone of their dignity the way a bad merchant cheats them of money.

424.title: Behar: hold him before he falls (Leviticus 25:35)
424.hook: support a struggling neighbor before he falls; Maimonides calls this the highest giving
424.howItsDone: Jewish communities run free-loan societies, job networks and quiet support funds often linked to this verse; Maimonides' eight levels of giving, from the Mishneh Torah's laws of gifts to the poor, are widely taught, with helping someone become self-supporting at the top.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ona'at devarim, wronging with words. Your line was words can wrong. Today, the last teaching of Behar, and a load starting to slip.

A donkey on a dirt road with a heavy sack on its back. The sack starts to slip. One person walking alongside can put a hand on it and push it back into place. Easy. Now let it fall. It's in the dust, split open, grain everywhere, and even five people together can't heave it back up. The picture comes from an old rabbinic commentary on a single verse in this week's portion. It isn't about donkeys. It's about the moment a neighbor's life starts to slip.
screen: `A SACK STARTS TO SLIP.` → `ONE HAND CAN HOLD IT.` → `ONCE IT FALLS, FIVE CAN'T.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-five, verse thirty-five, still in Behar. If your brother grows poor and his means begin to fail beside you, "then thou shalt uphold him". In Hebrew, v'hechezakta bo: take hold of him, strengthen him. The ancient commentary called the Sifra, and Rashi after it, read the verb with care. It doesn't say lift him up off the ground. It says hold him, which only works while he's still standing. That's where the donkey comes from: catch the load while it's slipping, because once it's down, it takes a crowd. Moses Maimonides wrote out eight levels of giving to the poor, from the one who gives grudgingly at the bottom to the very top. And the top rung isn't the biggest donation, or even the anonymous one. It's this verse: strengthen someone before they need to ask, with a gift, a loan, a partnership, or finding them work, so they can stand on their own. He quotes thou shalt uphold him as the proof. So the highest form of charity isn't a rescue. It's prevention. It happens quietly, before anyone has to stand in a line or fill out a form or say the hard words, I need help. It keeps a person's dignity whole, and keeps them a neighbor instead of a case. The verse goes on: let him live with thee. Not beneath you. With you.

segments.voice: Let faces come to mind: a friend who's gone quiet, a coworker whose hours were cut, a relative carrying more than they say. Notice whose load seems to be slipping. Then think of one small way to put a hand on the sack, an introduction, a ride, a meal, a lead on a job, a message that says I noticed, and hold that person in mind for a while.
Behar, the portion on the mountain. One of its teachings: strengthen a neighbor while they're still standing. The next portion begins tomorrow.
Your line: hold him before he falls. One hand, early, does what five can't do later. That's four hundred twenty-four days.

425.title: Bechukotai: if ye walk (Leviticus 26:3)
425.hook: the blessings begin with walking in God's ways
425.tomorrow: Bechukotai: I will walk among you (Leviticus 26:12)
425.howItsDone: Bechukotai is the last portion of Leviticus, read in the spring and often paired with Behar. The idea that Jewish law is a halachah, a way of walking, runs through Jewish teaching about daily practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Behar ended with a hand on a slipping load. Your line was hold him before he falls. Today, the last portion of Leviticus.

Jewish law, in Hebrew, is halachah. You'd guess it means rules, or code. It comes from the verb to walk, halach. The walk. The going. Not a building you live inside, not a wall you stay behind. A road. Today's portion, the last in Leviticus, opens its long list of blessings with that same verb. Before the rain, before the harvest, before peace, comes a single condition, and it's a way of moving.
screen: `HALACHAH: THE WALK.` → `NOT A WALL. A ROAD.` → `THE BLESSINGS START WITH WALKING.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-six, verse three: "If ye walk in My statutes, and keep My commandments, and do them". The portion takes its name from that verse: Bechukotai, in My statutes. What follows is a cascade. Rain in its season. Trees heavy with fruit. Threshing that runs until the grape harvest, and grape harvest until sowing, so the work of the year never quite catches up with the plenty. Peace in the land. You'll lie down, and none shall make you afraid. But the commentators stopped at the first line. The Sifra, the ancient rabbinic reading of Leviticus, asks: keep My commandments and do them is already in the verse, so what does if ye walk in My statutes add? Its answer, which Rashi repeats: toiling in Torah. Learning that costs some effort, the way a long walk costs some breath. Another strand of reading hears something else in the verb. You don't walk in a place once. A walk is daily, repeated, step after step, the ordinary distance between your door and the bus. Blessing, in this reading, isn't promised to a single heroic moment. It's attached to a pace. Some readers link the word for statutes, chukim, to a root that means to engrave, to cut into stone. Read that way, the line holds a tension. What's carved, you walk in. The fixed thing becomes a path.
screen: `IF YE WALK IN MY STATUTES.` · `RAIN, FRUIT, PEACE.` · `THE SIFRA: TOILING IN TORAH.` · `CARVED, AND STILL A PATH.` · then, large: `WALK IN THEM.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk slowly, even just across a room and back; if you can't, let your feet press the floor in turn, left, right, left. With each step, ask one quiet question: where are my daily steps actually pointing this year? Not where I'm supposed to be, but where I'm headed.
Bechukotai. In My statutes: the last portion of Leviticus, whose blessings begin with the verb to walk.
Your line: walk in them. A road, taken one ordinary step at a time. See you on the path tomorrow.

426.title: Bechukotai: I will walk among you (Leviticus 26:12)
426.hook: the promise is closeness: "I will walk among you"
426.howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads Leviticus 26:12 as a promise of God's closeness; the Sifra's reading, that God will walk with the people as one of them and they will not be afraid, is often taught alongside the verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday the blessings began with a verb. Your line was walk in them. Now, the same verb, turned around.

A good wedding toast builds. One wish, then another, each a little warmer, and the room waits for the big finish. The blessings in Leviticus twenty-six build the same way. Bread to the full. Sleep with no one to make you afraid. By the end, a listener might expect the biggest wish of all to be something you could weigh, or count, or lock in a barn. The last one in the run can't be stored. It's company. Yesterday the people walked in God's statutes. Today it's God who walks.
screen: `A TOAST THAT BUILDS.` → `THE LAST WISH IN THE RUN.` → `NOT A HARVEST. COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Leviticus twenty-six, verses eleven and twelve. First, God says the sanctuary will be set among the people. Then: "And I will walk among you, and will be your God, and ye shall be My people." The Hebrew verb is v'hithalachti, a form that means walking about, strolling, going to and fro. Not a march: the walk of someone at home. The same form appears in Genesis, where God is heard walking in the garden in the cool of the day. The Sifra, and Rashi after it, make the link out loud. I will stroll with you in the garden, God says, as one of you, and you won't tremble before Me. Closeness without terror. That's a surprising promise in a book full of fire and holy boundaries, where even the high priest is warned not to walk into the inner room whenever he likes. The next verse finishes the thought. I broke the bars of your yoke, God says, and made you walk upright. The people who once walked bent under Egyptian loads now walk with their heads up, and God walks among them. So the blessing at the top of the list isn't a thing. It's a relationship. The harvest is good. Company on the road is better.

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or soften them, and walk your street in your mind: the curb, the corner, the house with the loud dog, the bus stop. Where on that ordinary route have you seen kindness, beauty, patience, someone helping someone? If you pray, hold those places in that prayer; if you don't, simply notice that your street holds more than you usually see.
Bechukotai, the last portion of Leviticus. Its highest blessing: not a full barn, but God walking among the people, as one at home.
Your line: walking among you. At home, at an easy pace. Day four hundred twenty-six.

427.title: Bechukotai: hard words, softly
427.hook: the chapter of warnings is traditionally read quickly and quietly in synagogue
427.howItsDone: In many synagogues the warnings of Leviticus 26 are read as a single unit, in a lower voice and a quicker chant; often no one is called to that reading by name, and the reader or a volunteer takes it.

segments.voice: Yesterday the blessings reached their top: God walking among the people. Your line was walking among you. Today, the hard half of the chapter.

Sit in a synagogue on the Shabbat this portion is read, and at one point you might notice the room change. The reader has been chanting at a steady, clear volume. Then, partway through Leviticus twenty-six, the voice drops. The pace quickens. The words are still audible to anyone listening closely, but they go by low and fast, like someone hurrying through a hard paragraph in a letter. At the end of that stretch, the voice comes back up to full strength. Nobody announces it. It's a custom, and it's teaching something.
screen: `THE READER'S VOICE DROPS.` → `LOW AND FAST.` → `THEN, FULL VOICE AGAIN.`

segments.voice: After the blessings comes the other side. If the people refuse the covenant, the chapter lists what will follow: fear, failed harvests, enemies, exile, a land left empty. One line says the sound of a driven leaf will send people running. Jewish tradition calls this passage the tochacha, the rebuke, or the warning. The word shares a root with the command in Leviticus nineteen to rebuke your neighbor rather than nurse a grudge. So how do you read a rebuke aloud to a whole congregation? The customs around it are careful. The Talmud rules that the passage of curses isn't broken into pieces; it's read as one portion, without stopping in the middle. In many synagogues no one is called up to it by name. The reader takes it, or someone volunteers, so no one feels singled out for the curses. And it's read in that lowered, quicker voice. Not skipped. Not softened into something else. Every word is read, the way you'd tell someone something hard they need to hear: without drama, without relish. The rabbis taught the same about rebuke between people. Speak, because silence can be a failure of love. But a rebuke that shames someone in public is itself a wrong. The tochacha is a whole chapter of hard words. The custom gives it a gentle voice.
screen: `AFTER BLESSING, WARNING.` · `TOCHACHA: THE REBUKE.` · `ONE READING, NO ONE SINGLED OUT.` · `EVERY WORD, IN A LOW VOICE.` · then, large: `HARD WORDS, SOFTLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing you've been avoiding, a medical result, a tough email, a critical review of your work, and don't open it yet. Just breathe, and decide how you'll read it: slowly, all the way through, without shouting at it or at yourself. If it's something hard you need to say to someone, rehearse it in your head in a low, steady voice.

Tochacha. The rebuke: Leviticus twenty-six's warnings, read whole, in a low voice. This week ran from proclaim liberty, through guests on the land, words that wrong, and a hand that holds, to walking with God, and now this.
Your line: hard words, softly. Every word said, none of them shouted. That's four hundred twenty-seven days.
